messages:
sarah: Quick question — we're wiring up GCP Cloud KMS for a Private deployment that lives in customer-project-A but our control plane service account runs in infra-project-B. What's the recommended pattern for access? cross-project key rings vs SA impersonation?
kevin: Short answer: avoid giving broad roles across projects. Two safe patterns: 1) Put the key ring in the same project as the SA that will call KMS (preferred), or 2) keep key ring in project-A but use a dedicated service account in project-A that the control plane can impersonate.
kevin: If you go with impersonation you need to grant the control plane SA iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator on the target SA, and give the target SA roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter on the specific cryptoKey. Example: 
```
# grant impersonate
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding target-sa@project-a.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --member="serviceAccount:controlplane@infra-project-b.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator"

# grant KMS usage on the key
gcloud kms keys add-iam-policy-binding my-key --location=us-central1 --keyring=my-ring --project=project-a \
  --member="serviceAccount:target-sa@project-a.iam.gserviceaccount.com" --role="roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter"
```
kevin: Note: scope the role to the cryptoKey resource, not the project. Least privilege matters for audits.
dan: Related: audit logging. For Private we often have the KMS project locked down so logs don't surface to our central workspace by default. Make sure to create a logging sink in project-A to export Cloud Audit Logs (admin/data/access) to the security-project or to a PubSub that our SIEM subscribes to. Example: 
```
gcloud logging sinks create sink-kms pubsub.googleapis.com/projects/security-project/topics/kms-audit --log-filter="resource.type=\"kms_key\"" --project=project-a
```
dan: Also enable "DATA_ACCESS" audit logs for Cloud KMS in IAM -> Audit Logs for the key project, otherwise you miss decrypt calls.
mike: Rotation caveats we saw: creating a new key version in KMS doesn't magically rewrap all previously-encrypted data. With envelope encryption we store the encrypted data key (EDK) and the key version id. For immediate full-rotation you must rewrap (decrypt+encrypt) every EDK, or accept lazy rewrap on next write/read. Lazy rewrap is often fine but document it for customers.
mike: Example rotate flow we use: 1) create new key version, 2) update default cryptoKeyVersion for new encrypts (if using 'primary'), 3) run background rewrap job that processes blobs and updates their metadata with new version. Keep audits of rewrap jobs.
sarah: For Private on-prem deployments where there is no direct internet egress, can we still use Cloud KMS?
kevin: Yes, via a small proxy/connector that runs in the customer's VPC (like our private-control-plane agent) which impersonates the in-project SA or uses workload identity. If fully air-gapped and Cloud KMS isn't allowed, then customers must provide an HSM/KMS reachable on the network or use our on-prem KMS option.
kevin: If using Workload Identity Federation (external identities) ensure the service account has only the KMS roles and that the federation pool is narrowly scoped.
kevin: One extra gotcha: if you impersonate, you need to handle token lifetime and token creation quotas. TokenCreator is powerful — audit who has it.
kevin: Also, consider grant-only-once approach: create a short-lived per-tenant SA and rotate that binding as part of offboarding.
dan: Ops/alerts: surface any KMS CryptoKey versions.create and cryptoKey encrypt/decrypt errors into a Redwood KMS alert channel, with links to the audit log entry. That helps triage bad permissions vs key misconfiguration.
infra-bot: deploy-bot: created test keyring my-ring in project-a (location us-central1) for sarah's experiment. :white_check_mark:
mike: Next steps: I can draft a tiny runbook with commands for (1) create keyring/key, (2) set up impersonation binding, (3) enable audit logs, (4) run a rewrap job. I'll post it in /docs/eng-security/kms-private-runbook.md and link here.
sarah: awesome — can you also include a note about expiration/rotation policy and required customer consents? some legal teams require 90d rotation or explicit approval.
mike: will do. I'll also include a small troubleshooting checklist: permission denied vs invalid key version vs network timeouts.
sarah: thanks everyone, this clarifies the tradeoffs. I'll pick the impersonation pattern for the POC and we'll iterate for production.
